source.title: The Effect of Batch Size on Contrastive Self-Supervised Speech Representation Learning

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream speech-recognition performance after varying self-supervised training data exposure, extending the downstream-scaling question to wav2vec 2.0 speech representation learning. It does not test the language-model pretraining-loss power laws themselves.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. when discussing scaling, but does not sweep language-model parameters, tokens, or compute, measure held-out cross-entropy, fit power laws, or test a compute-optimal parameter/token split. The relevant new results are WER after wav2vec 2.0 pretraining and ASR fine-tuning as pretraining batch size or amount of data seen changes. Rows below cover selected numeric conditions; the paper reports many more WER conditions.
record.test_reason: The study pretrains a single ~95M-parameter wav2vec 2.0 BASE speech model and varies batch size and iterations, then reports downstream ASR WER. It cites Kaplan et al. only in related work. It fits no power law, measures no language-model loss, and does not vary parameters or compute allocation. V6 concerns language models, so speech SSL WER is a different kind of system. V5 would cover speech, but needs a power-law form, which is never fitted. The results are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that total data seen during pretraining (batch size × iterations) is the most important factor for downstream WER. They also find that larger batches help at a fixed iteration count. Batch size can vary without penalty between a convergence floor (150 s) and a diminishing-returns ceiling (40 min). They suggest benchmarking SSL at a fixed amount of data seen.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies batch size and training duration for wav2vec 2.0 speech SSL, then evaluates ASR WER. It does not reproduce language-model loss-versus-parameter/token/compute scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Pretraining batch size and total data seen affect WER; fine-tuning label amount, test split, and decoding method also vary. The authors report that 80-minute batches can underperform 40-minute batches on test-other and that batch-size returns diminish.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed model size, downstream ASR WER after wav2vec 2.0 pretraining depends mainly on total hours of audio seen, almost regardless of the batch-size/iteration split. At 16.7k h, 10-min-label test-clean WER ranges 72.00–73.63. At 66.7k h, 100h-label test-clean WER ranges 8.63–9.29 (Table IV, Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In contrastive speech SSL, downstream performance is a function of total pretraining data seen (batch size × steps), not of batch size per se.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 400k iterations, larger pretraining batches give lower WER from 150 s up to about 40 min, with diminishing returns or slight degradation at 80 min (test-other, ≥10h labels). Gradient std plateaus near 40 min, a critical batch size. 87.5 s diverges but still beats scratch.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Speech SSL has a critical batch size (~40 min audio for wav2vec 2.0 BASE) beyond which larger batches give diminishing returns.

record.problems: Only one model architecture and one model size are studied. The authors use heuristics rather than a full learning-rate hyperparameter search and select runs/checkpoints by validation loss. The WER tables report no uncertainty estimates. The experiments concern speech SSL and downstream ASR, not language-model cross-entropy power laws.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional Table III combinations of fine-tuning label amount, test split, and decoding, and additional Table IV test-other values and data-exposure settings. These were not included because of the 60-row limit; selected numeric WER conditions and the reported batch-size exception were retained. See Tables III and IV and Figures 3 and 5.

untested.parts: Whether a power-law form holds for speech SSL. WER falls with hours seen (Fig. 5, log x-axis), but no fit or exponent is reported.
Downstream predictability for language models. Only a speech model at one size is studied.
No LM held-out loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No fitted exponents compared; learning-rate heuristics are a setup choice, but no scaling law is fitted.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed: the system is a speech SSL model, not a language model, and no power-law or predictive fit is made. The learning rate was chosen heuristically among three options per batch size, and only one 80-min run was tried. No uncertainty estimates are given. The data-seen axis uses upper-bound hours.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or power-law relation in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No power-law fit or extrapolation from smaller to larger language-model runs is tested.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation is tested.
Architecture shape is not varied at a fixed parameter count.
The study uses speech SSL, but does not test whether a power-law loss form holds in speech or other modalities or training regimes.

Tests downstream ASR WER for one wav2vec 2.0 BASE model, on LibriSpeech, after varying pretraining batch size and observed data. It does not test language-model downstream tasks, downstream performance as a function of parameter count, or a fitted relation between pretraining loss and downstream performance.
Learning-rate and batch-size setup choices are discussed, but the study does not test fitted scaling exponents, compute-optimal allocations, or whether scaling curves depart from power laws.
